questions.prompt: How does a type declare that it satisfies an interface in Go?

options.text: It doesn't — satisfaction is implicit if it has the methods
By registering with the interface at startup

questions.explanation: Go uses structural typing: any type with all of an interface's methods satisfies it, with no declaration.

questions.prompt: When is an interface value equal to nil?

options.text: Only when both its type and its value are nil
Whenever the value inside is nil
Whenever the type is a pointer

questions.explanation: An interface holds a (type, value) pair and is nil only if both are nil; a nil concrete pointer stored in it gives it a type, so it is non-nil — the typed-nil gotcha.

questions.prompt: The empty interface, spelled ____ since Go 1.18, is satisfied by every type.
questions.explanation: `any` is an alias for `interface{}`; because it requires no methods, every type satisfies it.

questions.prompt: Why should you use `v, ok := x.(T)` instead of `v := x.(T)`?

options.text: The comma-ok form returns ok=false on mismatch instead of panicking
The single-value form is faster and safer
The comma-ok form is required by the compiler

questions.explanation: A single-value type assertion panics if the type doesn't match; the comma-ok form reports failure via the boolean instead.

questions.prompt: Which are good interface practices in Go? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep interfaces small (often one or two methods)
Accept interfaces and return concrete types
Define interfaces where they are used
Return a nil typed pointer as an error for success

questions.explanation: Small, use-site interfaces and accept-interfaces/return-structs are idiomatic. Returning a typed nil pointer as an error is the classic bug — return literal nil instead.

questions.prompt: Match each tool to what it does with an interface value.

pairs.right: Hold a value of any type
Let a type control how it prints

questions.explanation: Assertions and type switches inspect the concrete type; `any` holds anything; implementing Stringer customizes printing.
